When the psalm was written is disputed as usual. Calvin takes it of David congratulating the church that a seat had at last been appointed for the ark, carried about since Moses for a thousand years as if in pilgrimage; and he quotes Jebb on the play on the word for peace running through the poem, and on the argument for Davidic authorship — the fond mention of David's beloved city, the thrones of his house, and the recurrence of that peace promised as the blessing for his son. Clarke reads it of the captives returning after the edict of Cyrus: seventy years exiled, their heart in Jerusalem and their feet in Chaldea, their first thanksgiving for the kindness that let them home to his ordinances. Delitzsch explains only why the collector set it after a psalm that begins from the mountains, and notes that the ascription to David is missing from the chief Greek copies.

The gladness itself draws the closest reading. Spurgeon fixes on a single word: it was not go but let us go, and the ear found a double joy in it — glad for others, that they wished to go and had the courage to invite him, and glad that good people thought enough of him to ask. Henry presses the point into a rule: we should not only agree with one another but stir one another up — not do you go and pray for us while we stay at home, nor do you go first and we will follow at leisure. Calvin's joy is double for another reason. What delighted David was seeing the whole people concur with the oracle; our joy should likewise be doubled when God frames not only each of us but others with us to the obedience of his word, human nature being so stubborn that the majority murmur whenever he speaks. Calvin also disputes the versions, holding that the Greek and Latin give the second verb a neuter sense and so vitiate the meaning. Augustine turns the ascent into the whole subject: the degrees are not of descent but of ascent, and what the singer longs for is the eternal Jerusalem where the angels are our fellow-citizens. We sigh in the pilgrimage and shall rejoice in the city; and we find companions on the road who have already seen her and summon us to run.

The second verse turns on a tense. Ellicott corrects the future to a present already begun — our feet have been and are now standing, here we stand at last at thy gates — and bids us imagine the pilgrims halting to gaze about them as they arrive. Gill takes the standing spiritually, of attendance at the gates of wisdom, and looks past them to the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem.

What compact together means is the real crux. Gill and Clarke both take it of the fabric — the upper and lower city joined, the houses contiguous rather than straggling, every part contributing to the strength of the whole — and both move at once to the church, compact when its citizens are united in affection. Ellicott sets out three possibilities: the rebuilding of parts disconnected in the destruction; or, better, a countryman's astonishment on first seeing a compact city after a life among straggling villages, which he compares with Virgil's shepherd on Rome; or, most satisfactory, the Greek reading, which takes the word as a noun meaning union — she is the rallying point of the tribes. Delitzsch confirms that from the next verse, where the twelve tribes, still distinguished after the exile, come together at the three great feasts. On the testimony Ellicott calls the Authorised Version erroneous and makes the words parenthetical, an ordinance for Israel; Wesley and Clarke identify it with the ark, named from the tables laid up in it.

The thrones are read as courts first of all. Gill and Clarke take them of the courts of judicature in the city, and Clarke adds a condition: while the thrones of the house of David were there, the people had justice. Wesley distinguishes the royal throne allotted to David and his posterity from the inferior seats under his authority, and makes the courts supreme in ecclesiastical and civil affairs. Ellicott turns the mention into evidence about date. The city, first a cause of wonder, is now admired as the capital; the phrase house of David disposes of the psalm's title but does not prove the monarchy still standing, since even the later council might administer justice from the throne of David's successors. He notes that administering justice was the original duty of a monarch in peace, and that the margin's do sit gives the literal Hebrew, which uses sit where English would say stand — exactly, he says, as provincial Scotch does.

The petition that follows is the hinge of the psalm, and Delitzsch takes the idiom apart. To ask someone's peace is to find out his prosperity by asking, to be glad it is well with him, and so to be animated by the wish that he may prosper; in Syriac the phrase means simply to salute. The poet, calling up the picture of his country's city of peace, spreads his hands over it from afar and calls on his countrymen everywhere to salute it. Clarke hears the sound as well as the sense: there is a remarkable alliteration here, one Hebrew letter recurring through the clause, and sets beside it the alliterative manner of older English poetry, quoting Piers Plowman and Milton on the far-off curfew swinging slow with sullen roar.

Henry makes the passage a discipline of prayer. Those who can do nothing else for the peace of Jerusalem can pray for it, which is more than showing goodwill — it is the appointed way of fetching in mercy; and we must pray not out of custom nor for fashion but from a principle of love, since in seeking the public welfare we seek our own. Peace within thy walls covers all the inhabitants from least to greatest, and asks that the fortifications be never attacked, or if attacked never taken; prosperity within thy palaces covers the rulers, for if they prosper it will be well for the public — and the poorer sort, apt to envy that prosperity, are taught to pray for it. He also catches what David does not say. He does not say, let others pray for the public peace, the priests and prophets whose business it is, while I fight for it and rule for it; he says he will pray for it too, and second the prayers with endeavours, since whatever lies within our sphere for the public good we must do, or the prayer is insincere.

Gill reads the walls as the church's defences and reports the Targum's alternative, in thine army, making the petition a wish of success to the church militant. Ellicott notes that the formal greeting now appears, the one that greets every traveller in the East, and that the religious motive is held back to the last verse and made more emphatic by the delay. Gill and Clarke insist the motive is not private: not David's own palace or family, but the sanctuary and the worship carried on in it; and Gill observes that David, though a king, reckoned his meanest spiritual subjects his brethren and companions. Clarke closes with an application. He recalls the prophet's charge to the captives to seek the peace of the city where they were carried, since in its prosperity they should prosper; asks whether that is not every man's duty to his own country; and says of those who instead raise seditions that hemp would be disgraced by hanging them.
